sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.11730.question: For LLaMA pretraining, how were spectral weight decay and standard weight decay matched on validation loss, training compute, and SVD-LLM compression settings, and what compression and inference-speed results were measured?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. passages.text: We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

We used a variety of compute resources with different GPU hardware, including RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti Super, RTX A500, RTX A6000, 40GB A100, 80GB A100, H100, MI100, and MI210. For the large model pre-training, such as the 350M and 1B LLaMA model pre-training experiments, we trained the model on nodes equipped with 4 H100 or 4 MI210.

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

On the other hand, although O-LDAdam yields a slightly longer average update time than LDAdam with T = 200 T=200 due to the need to perform power iterations multiple times ( Algorithm 3 ), the additional cost is not prohibitively large. Moreover, O-LDAdam demonstrates a nontrivial speedup compared to the standard LDAdam setting with a per-step update schedule ( T = 1 T=1 ). Together with the model performance results shown in Table 2 , this demonstrates that O-LDAdam strikes a good balance between model performance and computational cost in the extremely low-rank regime. Table 11 presents the full results of memory and Wallclock time comparison of all the optimizer methods on the LLaMA model pre-training task on the C4 dataset. As shown by the table, our method Ori achieves superior memory and computation time profile almost across the broad, demonstrating its general efficiency under various settings. Table 11 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison of pre-training various sized LLaMa model on the C4 dataset.

passages.text: However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

The descent itself is genuine, since the DeiT-Tiny and ViT-Tiny sweeps keep falling past the peak once extended to 4 ​ d 4d ; what the paired column adds is its price, a gap that narrows only from above and only slowly, so wherever it closes at all it closes far outside the range where the adapter was still cheaper than dense. The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and alignment assumptions support the singular-mode results for GD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC, and what empirical tests validate or limit those predictions in neural-network or language-model training?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . As a result, the ordering of saturation rates across target modes need not agree with GD. The right panel shows precisely this effect. For L = 2 L=2 , β \beta decreases with μ \mu , so smaller target modes saturate faster than larger ones. For L = 8 L=8 , the trend reverses and larger target modes saturate faster. The case L = 4 L=4 lies near the transition and becomes weakly nonmonotone. This depth driven change in ordering is the clearest empirical instance of the Shampoo mode reversal predicted by the theory.

Figs. 9 and 11 show the evolution of training loss and ranks throughout training for depths L = 2 L=2 and 8 8 , respectively. Nevertheless, the stable and effective ranks evolve differently. Thus similar terminal predictors need not imply similar spectral learning dynamics. We train the same deep linear predictor on an underdetermined, nonwhitened regression problem using GD, Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and KFAC. All methods reach comparable final loss and final spectra of W W despite substantially different transient dynamics shown by the stable rank and effective rank throughout training. The optimizer geometry strongly changes how quickly spectral mass concentrates.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 17 make this distinction particularly clear. GD exhibits pronounced separation between the emergence times of successive singular values, consistent with the factorization induced small mode barrier derived in the aligned setting. Adam substantially compresses these delays. Muon produces a markedly more synchronized growth of the singular spectrum, consistent with normalization reducing mode dependent mobility differences. Cumulative Shampoo also accelerates weaker spectral components after its preconditioner has accumulated sufficient history, while K-FAC produces comparatively smooth growth across the spectrum through curvature correction. These effects remain visible even though the singular vectors are not fixed and the data covariance couples the modes. The experiment therefore supports the interpretation of the theoretical phase laws as mechanisms governing transient spectral learning rather than merely properties of the special aligned model. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 17: Singular value trajectories in nonaligned underdetermined linear regression. Although all methods approach similar final singular spectra, their transient spectrum differ substantially. The qualitative optimizer dependent dynamics predicted by the aligned phase analysis remain visible even when the empirical data covariance couples singular directions and the exact scalar mode reduction no longer holds.

inspect:2611.07859.question: In the controlled closed-search comparisons, how were CORE, Tongyi DeepResearch, and OpenResearcher matched for retrieval corpus, agent models, tool-call or token budgets, and context size, and what answer-accuracy and evidence-recall results were measured?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Table 1: Main comparison results. Answer accuracy and evidence recall are in percent. Peak context is the median, over questions, of the maximum context length in tokens. Tokens/search is the mean number of tokens returned per search call, summed over all subqueries. Search calls is the mean number of search calls per question. Token counts are comparable only within the same agent model. Arrows show the preferred direction, and bold marks the best value in each of these columns within each model–benchmark group. We find that Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, using the original Tongyi DeepResearch harness with document-level retrieval based on AgentIR-4B, achieves 63.13% on BrowseComp-Plus, which is lower than the 65.66% achieved by our current passage-level retrieval setup. On BrowseComp-Plus, Jiang et al. (2026) report an evidence recall of 38.1% for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, whereas their Harness-1 (20B) reported the evidence recall at 58.4%.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Table 1: Main comparison results. Answer accuracy and evidence recall are in percent. Peak context is the median, over questions, of the maximum context length in tokens. Tokens/search is the mean number of tokens returned per search call, summed over all subqueries. Search calls is the mean number of search calls per question. Token counts are comparable only within the same agent model. Arrows show the preferred direction, and bold marks the best value in each of these columns within each model–benchmark group. We find that Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, using the original Tongyi DeepResearch harness with document-level retrieval based on AgentIR-4B, achieves 63.13% on BrowseComp-Plus, which is lower than the 65.66% achieved by our current passage-level retrieval setup. On BrowseComp-Plus, Jiang et al. (2026) report an evidence recall of 38.1% for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, whereas their Harness-1 (20B) reported the evidence recall at 58.4%.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

We compare Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B and OpenResearcher-30B-A3B ( Li et al., 2026b ) under CORE on BrowseComp-Plus. Both use the same corpus, passage index, retrieval and context-management configuration, and GPT-5.5 judge at high reasoning effort. Sampling parameters follow Appendix A.2 ; context budgets and tool-call formats follow each model’s configuration. Table 3 shows higher answer accuracy for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B in this setting, supporting its selection for the main experiments. Agent model Answer accuracy (%) ↑ \uparrow Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B 80.12 OpenResearcher-30B-A3B 62.41 Table 3: Deep research agents evaluated with CORE on BrowseComp-Plus. Accuracy is computed over all 830 questions; empty answers receive no credit. Bold marks the higher accuracy.

inspect:2610.08049.question: In language-model fine-tuning experiments, what held-out performance, peak GPU memory, and training time does the proposed Riemannian LoRA optimizer achieve versus vanilla LoRA and full fine-tuning at matched adapter rank, tuned learning rates, and training budget?

passages.text: Optimization. Several optimization approaches for LoRA have been proposed [ 56 , 69 , 26 , 41 ] . For example, Wang et al. [56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

Others. To improve the performance of LoRA, several LoRA variants have been proposed. Hayou et al. [19] applied different learning rates to B B and A A and shows fast convergence. Liu et al. [29] decomposed the pre-trained weight into magnitude and direction, and then employed LoRA for directional updates to reduce the number of trainable parameters. Xia et al. [59] trained multiple LoRA sequentially like the residual learning to improve the performance of LoRA. Dettmers et al. [11] applied quantization to the pre-trained models with LoRA to save memory usage without sacrificing performance. We leave the combination of these studies with our method to future work.

To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 . Figure 1: Training time comparison of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning.

In this paper, we proposed a Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. This metric induces new preconditioning, and we theoretically showed that this preconditioning makes LoRA better approximates full fine-tuning compared with the conventional preconditioning and no preconditioning. Diverse experiments showed the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning in the language and vision domains. This paper is the first to explore the possibility of tailoring a Riemannian metric to LoRA, paving the way for future followers.

We provide the details of hyperparameters used in our experiments to ensure reproducibility. For each task, all compared methods share a common set of hyperparameters, such as the rank, batch size, weight decay, and training schedule, which are outlined in Sec. 7 . When decoding a sentence in Sec. 7.2 , we used the beam search with the beam size to 10 10 , the length penalty to 0.8 0.8 , and the no-repeat-Ngram-size to 4 4 , following [ 63 ] . For answer generation in Sec. 7.4 , we used greedy decoding with a maximum of 30 generated tokens. As mentioned in Sec. 7 , we individually tune the learning rate for each method on each validation set to ensure fair comparison. Table 6 lists the tuned learning rates for the natural language generation task in Sec. 7.2 . In this task, we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. Tables 7 and 8 list the tuned learning rates for the image classification task in Sec. 7.3 and the commonsense reasoning task in Sec. 7.4 , respectively. In these tasks, we tuned the learning rate over { 0.0001 , 0.0002 , … , 0.001 } \{0.0001,0.0002,\dots,0.001\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. Note that, in the natural language generation task of Sec. 7.2 , we selected the learning rate that achieves the highest average rank (and the lowest rank variance in case of ties in the highest average rank) across the five evaluation metrics (BLEU [ 40 ] , NIST [ 12 ] , METEOR [ 3 ] , ROUGE-L [ 27 ] , and CIDEr [ 53 ] ) on the validation set. inspect:2611.17191.question: In the three-model mixed-domain LoRA rank sweeps, what held-out perplexity and forgetting results does Rényi-2 effective-rank regularization achieve versus unpenalized LoRA at matched rank, training budget, and tuned penalty? What training-time or memory overhead is measured?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

We first evaluate whether increasing adapter effective rank mitigates the learning–forgetting trade-off in a heterogeneous supervised fine-tuning setting that proxies continual learning. We report the Roy–Vetterli effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) of the accumulated update (higher indicates fuller use of available adapter capacity), training-mixture perplexity (Train PPL), and perplexity on the retention probes described above. This reported diagnostic differs from the Rényi-2 surrogate optimized by the penalty. Lower perplexity is better throughout. Figure 2 summarizes all methods across adapter capacity (panel A) and the learning–forgetting trade-off (panels B–D). The favorable region in the trade-off panels is the lower-left corner (strong learning with limited forgetting). Appendix Table 5 reports the full numbers; entries with ± \pm are means and sample standard deviations over three training executions, except PiSSA ( n = 2 n=2 ), and the remaining rows are single runs. PiSSA excludes one resumed execution with apparent data replay (Appendix G.1 ); its small two-run SD does not establish low population variability.

Figure 2: Dense FT denotes dense down-projection fine-tuning. Mixed-domain continual-learning baselines on Qwen2.5-0.5B (base, not Instruct; rank r = 896 r{=}896 unless noted). Each point represents a method–penalty configuration; the legend maps dot colors to adapter type. Points show multi-run means or single-run endpoints; sample SDs are reported in Appendix Table 5 . (A) Effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) shown as a vertical strip from 0 0 to nominal rank 896 896 (horizontal dashed line), with horizontal offsets only for visibility; higher indicates fuller adapter capacity utilization. (B–D) Learning–forgetting trade-offs: Train PPL (mixture learning) versus Wiki PPL, StarCoder PPL (pretraining proxies), and WMT CS–EN PPL (in-mixture translation retention); lower-left is better. The three Rényi-2 penalty points use different regularization weights λ \lambda . Unpenalized PiSSA and LoRA-XS have the highest Wiki perplexities; VeRA, SVF, and TinyLoRA limit forgetting with weaker mixture fit. NB-LoRA approaches the λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 learning–retention trade-off. Unpenalized PiSSA uses two runs after excluding one resumed execution with apparent data replay; the other multi-run points use three executions. Dense FT, LoRA at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , and penalized PiSSA at λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 are single runs. Full numeric values and the PiSSA exclusion are documented in Appendix Table 5 and its accompanying text.

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

inspect:2610.20857.question: How were IDEA2PRIOR and the ChatGPT/Gemini Deep Research baselines evaluated on EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD paper-retrieval queries? What were the ground-truth criteria, candidate and evidence budgets, and per-difficulty Hit@5 results?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

Quantization-aware training (QAT) inserts the quantizer into the forward pass and updates latent full-precision weights through the straight-through estimator (STE) ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) . At low bit widths it recovers much of the accuracy lost by post-training quantization (PTQ) ( Frantar et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) , both when fine-tuning a pretrained checkpoint ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) and when training from scratch ( Panferov et al., 2025 ; Tabesh et al., 2025 ) . This accuracy comes at a memory cost. QAT keeps full-precision weights and gradients, and most recipes rely on AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) , which stores two FP32 moments and adds 8 ​ n ​ m 8nm bytes for each n × m n\times m weight matrix. A natural remedy is to borrow memory-efficient optimizers from full-precision training. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) project the gradient onto a rank- r r subspace, keep Adam states only in that subspace, and map the update back to the full space. This works well when the optimization signal is concentrated in a few directions. Figure 1 shows that the same strategy does not carry over to QAT. With rank 64 and tuned learning rates, both methods are clearly worse than AdamW, in from-scratch training as well as in fine-tuning. We hypothesize that this is a property of the QAT update itself. Under the STE, the gradient has to compensate for element-wise quantization errors, which are spread over individual entries rather than aligned with a few directions of the weight matrix. If these corrections are less concentrated in the top- r r subspace than the rest of the update, a projection-based optimizer discards them at every step, and no amount of tuning inside the subspace recovers them.

Figure 1: WikiText-2 perplexity versus optimizer state memory for different optimizers under two QAT paradigms. The x-axis reports the total optimizer state size of the full model (in GB). All experiments use W2A16 quantization with group size 128, and projection-based optimizers use rank 64. For a fair comparison, the learning rate of each optimizer is tuned via grid search and the best result is reported. To address this limitation, we decompose the QAT optimization signal according to its geometric structure. We apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the dense global momentum, retaining the top- r r singular vectors to form the orthonormal bases U t ∈ ℝ n × r U_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} and V t ∈ ℝ m × r V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} . These bases induce a principal matrix subspace 𝒮 t = { U t ​ A ​ V t ⊤ : A ∈ ℝ r × r } \mathcal{S}_{t}=\left\{U_{t}AV_{t}^{\top}:A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\right\} . The momentum can then be exactly decomposed into its projection onto 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and an orthogonal residual lying in 𝒮 t ⟂ \mathcal{S}_{t}^{\perp} . The principal projection captures the dominant low-rank structure of the optimization trajectory, whereas the orthogonal residual retains dispersed signals outside the principal subspace. Our empirical results show that these residual signals become particularly important under QAT. Their magnitude matters little: keeping only their sign, with no second-moment state, recovers most of the lost quality (Section 5.1 ).

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 3: Comparison of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput across different models. Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

passages.text: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) tasks, comparing its optimization and downstream performance against existing LoRA optimizers. We describe the experimental setup in Section 4.1 , present the SFT and RL results in Section 4.2 and 4.3 , respectively, and further study the contribution of its components and its sensitivity to learning-rate selection in Section 4.4 . (a) Llama-3.2-3B (b) Llama-3.1-8B Figure 1: Validation loss (mean cross-entropy across response tokens) over the last 100 training steps on the math SFT task at rank r = 16 r=16 (see Appendix C for the r = 32 r=32 case and additional results across different ranks).

We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. selections.summary: CORE is a training-free research harness that retrieves passages, returns selected snippets, supports source-context expansion, and suppresses repeated snippets. Its inspected closed-search comparisons report higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than two harness baselines across three agent models and benchmarks.
selections.relevance: Directly applicable to retrieval and context management in a handwritten research-digest harness.

evidence.quote: Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison

selections.summary: Idea2Prior combines candidate discovery, identity verification, abstract assessment, citation expansion, and joint ranking. In a small historical retrieval comparison, reported Hit@5 is 16/30 overall, with the advantage concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM queries rather than HARD.
selections.relevance: Informs auditable paper retrieval, ranking, and evaluation for the digest agent.

evidence.quote: The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research.
The small, overlapping target set and historical protocol do not support a broad or statistically established superiority claim.

limitations: Findings are paper-reported; independent replication was not assessed.
Code links mentioned in papers were not verified as complete or runnable implementations.
Monarch–Muon quality and 6.9B systems measurements come from different comparisons; structured and dense representations are not identical.
The CORE and Idea2Prior evaluations concern research or paper retrieval, not this digest harness specifically.

2610.11730:9ae9804c9388362251b1a40d2dbba.question: For LLaMA pretraining, how were spectral weight decay and standard weight decay matched on validation loss, training compute, and SVD-LLM compression settings, and what compression and inference-speed results were measured?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

The compression results in Section 3 use SVD-LLM. We compare five singular-value-based compression methods on one checkpoint to select this method. Table 2 applies truncated SVD, SliceGPT [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] , ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] , SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , and Dobi-SVD [ Wang et al., 2025 ] to a 124 124 M-parameter spectral-weight-decay model with coefficient 1 1 . We also report accuracy on ARC-Easy [ Clark et al., 2018 ] , HellaSwag [ Zellers et al., 2019 ] , and PIQA [ Bisk et al., 2020 ] after compression. Truncated SVD reaches 1.43 × 1.43\times compression with a + 0.0359 +0.0359 validation-loss increase. SliceGPT produces a larger loss increase at a lower compression rate. ASVD and SVD-LLM preserve validation loss better at comparable compression, with increases of + 0.0286 +0.0286 and + 0.0196 +0.0196 , respectively. Dobi-SVD reaches a similar + 0.0207 +0.0207 increase at 1.21 × 1.21\times compression. SVD-LLM gives the lowest validation loss among the compressed models, so we use it throughout.
