BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

passages.text: We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

We used a variety of compute resources with different GPU hardware, including RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti Super, RTX A500, RTX A6000, 40GB A100, 80GB A100, H100, MI100, and MI210. For the large model pre-training, such as the 350M and 1B LLaMA model pre-training experiments, we trained the model on nodes equipped with 4 H100 or 4 MI210.

Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

Moreover, O-LDAdam demonstrates a nontrivial speedup compared to the standard LDAdam setting with a per-step update schedule ( T = 1 T=1 ). Together with the model performance results shown in Table 2 , this demonstrates that O-LDAdam strikes a good balance between model performance and computational cost in the extremely low-rank regime. passages.text: However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. 2610.04507:b858ce61dbc6ef65dc6a4fb7e6249.question: In the noisy-label experiments, how were LoRA rank sweeps matched to dense fine-tuning by modules, seeds, training budget, and parameter count, and what generalization results were measured for the 7B language model?

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. 2610.04249:eab50254c5958c5adb297db9f36ca.question: What balance and alignment assumptions support the singular-mode results for GD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC, and what empirical tests validate or limit those predictions in neural-network or language-model training?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Fig. 8 studies the decay exponent of unsupported modes and focuses on Shampoo saturation, where mode order reversal can happen theoretically. For decay, increasing depth changes the small mode geometry through p = 2 − 2 / L p=2-2/L . Empirically, GD, Adam, and cumulative Shampoo follow the predicted increase α d = p + 1 = 3 − 2 L , \alpha_{d}=p+1=3-\frac{2}{L}, so deeper factorizations produce a steeper polynomial tail near zero. In contrast, undamped K-FAC remains close to α d = 1 \alpha_{d}=1 , reflecting its exponential decay law, while Muon exhibits a much weaker depth dependence, consistent with its normalized geometry. Thus depth does not affect all optimizers uniformly: it strengthens the Euclidean style barrier for GD like methods, but has much less impact on normalized or curvature corrected decay. For saturation, we focus on cumulative Shampoo because it is the optimizer for which mode reversal can happen and depth also affects it. Its asymptotic saturation coefficient depends on both target size and accumulated history, β Sh ​ ( μ ) = L ​ μ p D ⋆ ​ ( μ ) . \beta_{\rm Sh}(\mu)=\dfrac{L\mu^{p}}{D_{\star}(\mu)}. As a result, the ordering of saturation rates across target modes need not agree with GD. The right panel shows precisely this effect. Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

2611.07859:97199b40ee70629c5ae8d1abb52cd.question: In the controlled closed-search comparisons, how were CORE, Tongyi DeepResearch, and OpenResearcher matched for retrieval corpus, agent models, tool-call or token budgets, and context size, and what answer-accuracy and evidence-recall results were measured?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Table 1: Main comparison results. Answer accuracy and evidence recall are in percent. Peak context is the median, over questions, of the maximum context length in tokens. Tokens/search is the mean number of tokens returned per search call, summed over all subqueries. Search calls is the mean number of search calls per question. Token counts are comparable only within the same agent model. Arrows show the preferred direction, and bold marks the best value in each of these columns within each model–benchmark group. We find that Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, using the original Tongyi DeepResearch harness with document-level retrieval based on AgentIR-4B, achieves 63.13% on BrowseComp-Plus, which is lower than the 65.66% achieved by our current passage-level retrieval setup. On BrowseComp-Plus, Jiang et al. (2026) report an evidence recall of 38.1% for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, whereas their Harness-1 (20B) reported the evidence recall at 58.4%.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

2610.08049:5ed2d0ede195d1e7f8535037c169a.question: In language-model fine-tuning experiments, what held-out performance, peak GPU memory, and training time does the proposed Riemannian LoRA optimizer achieve versus vanilla LoRA and full fine-tuning at matched adapter rank, tuned learning rates, and training budget?

passages.text: Optimization. Several optimization approaches for LoRA have been proposed [ 56 , 69 , 26 , 41 ] . For example, Wang et al. [56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

Others. To improve the performance of LoRA, several LoRA variants have been proposed. Hayou et al. [19] applied different learning rates to B B and A A and shows fast convergence. Liu et al. [29] decomposed the pre-trained weight into magnitude and direction, and then employed LoRA for directional updates to reduce the number of trainable parameters. Xia et al. [59] trained multiple LoRA sequentially like the residual learning to improve the performance of LoRA. Dettmers et al. [11] applied quantization to the pre-trained models with LoRA to save memory usage without sacrificing performance. We leave the combination of these studies with our method to future work.

To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 . Figure 1: Training time comparison of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning.

In this paper, we proposed a Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. This metric induces new preconditioning, and we theoretically showed that this preconditioning makes LoRA better approximates full fine-tuning compared with the conventional preconditioning and no preconditioning. Diverse experiments showed the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning in the language and vision domains. This paper is the first to explore the possibility of tailoring a Riemannian metric to LoRA, paving the way for future followers.

For each task, all compared methods share a common set of hyperparameters, such as the rank, batch size, weight decay, and training schedule, which are outlined in Sec. 7 . When decoding a sentence in Sec. 7.2 , we used the beam search with the beam size to 10 10 , the length penalty to 0.8 0.8 , and the no-repeat-Ngram-size to 4 4 , following [ 63 ] . For answer generation in Sec. 7.4 , we used greedy decoding with a maximum of 30 generated tokens. What training-time or memory overhead is measured?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

We first evaluate whether increasing adapter effective rank mitigates the learning–forgetting trade-off in a heterogeneous supervised fine-tuning setting that proxies continual learning. We report the Roy–Vetterli effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) of the accumulated update (higher indicates fuller use of available adapter capacity), training-mixture perplexity (Train PPL), and perplexity on the retention probes described above. This reported diagnostic differs from the Rényi-2 surrogate optimized by the penalty. Lower perplexity is better throughout. Figure 2 summarizes all methods across adapter capacity (panel A) and the learning–forgetting trade-off (panels B–D). The favorable region in the trade-off panels is the lower-left corner (strong learning with limited forgetting). Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

2610.20857:3c0f3f43b9d1f9d0590e3aa867aec.question: How were IDEA2PRIOR and the ChatGPT/Gemini Deep Research baselines evaluated on EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD paper-retrieval queries? What were the ground-truth criteria, candidate and evidence budgets, and per-difficulty Hit@5 results?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

passages.text: Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. 2611.08924:4ce1660e28f1c470aca446761fd3f.question: In LLM quantization-aware training, what peak total GPU training memory, throughput, and validation-quality results does ResQAdam achieve versus AdamW, GaLore, and LDAdam at matched models, training budgets, and hardware? Distinguish optimizer-state memory from total peak memory.

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

Quantization-aware training (QAT) inserts the quantizer into the forward pass and updates latent full-precision weights through the straight-through estimator (STE) ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) . At low bit widths it recovers much of the accuracy lost by post-training quantization (PTQ) ( Frantar et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) , both when fine-tuning a pretrained checkpoint ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) and when training from scratch ( Panferov et al., 2025 ; Tabesh et al., 2025 ) . This accuracy comes at a memory cost. QAT keeps full-precision weights and gradients, and most recipes rely on AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) , which stores two FP32 moments and adds 8 ​ n ​ m 8nm bytes for each n × m n\times m weight matrix. A natural remedy is to borrow memory-efficient optimizers from full-precision training. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) project the gradient onto a rank- r r subspace, keep Adam states only in that subspace, and map the update back to the full space. This works well when the optimization signal is concentrated in a few directions. Figure 1 shows that the same strategy does not carry over to QAT. With rank 64 and tuned learning rates, both methods are clearly worse than AdamW, in from-scratch training as well as in fine-tuning. We hypothesize that this is a property of the QAT update itself. Under the STE, the gradient has to compensate for element-wise quantization errors, which are spread over individual entries rather than aligned with a few directions of the weight matrix. If these corrections are less concentrated in the top- r r subspace than the rest of the update, a projection-based optimizer discards them at every step, and no amount of tuning inside the subspace recovers them.

Figure 1: WikiText-2 perplexity versus optimizer state memory for different optimizers under two QAT paradigms. The x-axis reports the total optimizer state size of the full model (in GB). All experiments use W2A16 quantization with group size 128, and projection-based optimizers use rank 64. For a fair comparison, the learning rate of each optimizer is tuned via grid search and the best result is reported. To address this limitation, we decompose the QAT optimization signal according to its geometric structure. We apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the dense global momentum, retaining the top- r r singular vectors to form the orthonormal bases U t ∈ ℝ n × r U_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} and V t ∈ ℝ m × r V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} . These bases induce a principal matrix subspace 𝒮 t = { U t ​ A ​ V t ⊤ : A ∈ ℝ r × r } \mathcal{S}_{t}=\left\{U_{t}AV_{t}^{\top}:A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\right\} . The momentum can then be exactly decomposed into its projection onto 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and an orthogonal residual lying in 𝒮 t ⟂ \mathcal{S}_{t}^{\perp} . The principal projection captures the dominant low-rank structure of the optimization trajectory, whereas the orthogonal residual retains dispersed signals outside the principal subspace. Our empirical results show that these residual signals become particularly important under QAT. Their magnitude matters little: keeping only their sign, with no second-moment state, recovers most of the lost quality (Section 5.1 ).

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 3: Comparison of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput across different models. Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

passages.text: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) tasks, comparing its optimization and downstream performance against existing LoRA optimizers. We describe the experimental setup in Section 4.1 , present the SFT and RL results in Section 4.2 and 4.3 , respectively, and further study the contribution of its components and its sensitivity to learning-rate selection in Section 4.4 . We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. We evaluate the finetuned model using greedy decoding on three held-out benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 examples), GSM8K test (1319 examples), and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) (674 examples). We tune Adam’s learning rate on a logarithmic grid and select 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . We use the same learning rate for RoM without further tuning.
